I'm testing a hypothesis that shapes made of 5-colored cells get recolored based on proximity to a colored marker, with markers removed afterward. Checking example 1, it looks like each marker cluster corresponds to and recolors its nearest shape.

Now I'm testing whether shape size determines coloring instead—counting cells in each shape across example 3 to see if the largest shapes (9 cells each) are the ones that get colored while smaller ones stay uncolored.

But example 2 breaks that theory: the colored cross shape only has 5 cells, while other uncolored shapes have more or fewer, so size alone doesn't explain it. I'm now wondering if the marker clusters encode a count that determines which shape gets selected instead.

In example 1 the six-cell shapes get colored, but that breaks in example 2 where the cross and L-shape are both five cells yet only the cross is marked, and the six-cell block stays uncolored — so it's not simply about size. I'm now wondering if the marker shapes themselves encode which shape to pick, checking whether the marker cluster's geometry matches the target shape's geometry.

I'm testing whether combining the two marker clusters' cell counts equals the size of the colored shape — cross has 5 cells and the two marker clusters add up to 5, in example 1 the clusters sum to 6 matching the colored shapes' size, and in example 3 they sum to 9 matching those colored shapes too.

But then I notice the L-shape in example 2 is also 5 cells, same as the cross, yet only the cross gets colored in the output — so cell count alone can't be the deciding rule, and only one shape ends up highlighted despite there being two clusters.

I try another angle: maybe the marker shapes combine somehow to point at the target, or maybe the rule is about symmetry — the cross has clean 4-fold symmetry while checking if the diamond shares that property but still isn't colored.

I wonder if proximity to the marker cluster matters instead, but nothing seems to line up rows 9-10 near the diamond region. Counting cells again, both the cross and the L-shape total five, matching the marker cell count too, which seems suspicious rather than meaningful — so I consider that this isn't the right rule after all.

Trying bounding boxes instead: shape A is 3x3=9 cells, shape B is 4x2=8, so that doesn't align cleanly either. Then I try decomposing shapes into L-trominoes — marker1 and marker2 in example 1 are each single L-trominoes, and the colored shapes A and B both seem to break down into two L-trominoes each, which feels like a promising pattern to check against example 3's markers.

Actually the marker cells aren't even contiguous shapes themselves - some are isolated or diagonal-only, so maybe they're not meant to be read as connected shapes at all. I'm trying counting distinct marker clusters instead, wondering if that number points to which colored shape to select.

Testing example 1: the marker near row1-2 cols8-9 sits close to shape B at rows6-9 cols7-8, and the marker at rows6-7 cols0-1 sits right next to shape A at cols2-4 rows7-9 — specifically (7,1) touches (7,2). So it seems like each marker is positioned adjacent to the shape it's meant to indicate, rather than matching its outline.

Checking example 2 breaks this though — the markers there aren't adjacent to any shape. I try another idea: maybe the marker's cell count matches the target shape's cell count, but that doesn't resolve cleanly either. I go back to recounting the cross shape's actual cells to double-check my grid reading.

Then I wonder if congruence between shapes matters instead — maybe the shapes that get colored are ones that are duplicated (congruent pairs) elsewhere in the grid, so I start comparing the cell coordinates of the two colored shapes in example 1 to see if they're the same shape rotated or reflected.

Actually there's a matching diagonal shape elsewhere that isn't colored, suggesting markers might indicate which shapes to exclude from coloring rather than which to include. Let me count marker clusters versus uncolored shapes across examples: in example 3 there are 3 marker clusters and 3 uncolored shapes, and in example 1 there are 2 clusters matching 2 uncolored shapes — that's promising. Checking ex3 diagonal cluster and two L-tromino clusters, giving 3 clusters matching 3 uncolored shapes. But I'm unsure the shapes match by form, so I'm considering whether the total marker cell count instead maps to something about the shapes being kept.

Maybe the rule relates to grid position instead — like which side or region the colored shapes occupy — but that doesn't hold across examples either. I'm now wondering if each marker cluster actually points toward a specific shape rather than just counting cells.

Wait, maybe markers are fragments that match a shape's corner shape elsewhere - like the marker cluster forms an L that appears as a piece within some shape, but which shape (colored or uncolored) seems inconsistent between examples, so that theory might not hold up.

Let me instead check cell counts: in Ex1 the markers total 6 cells and each colored shape also has 6 cells; in Ex3 markers total 9 and colored shapes also have 9. In Ex2 markers total 5, matching the cross shape's 5 cells, but the L-shape also appears to have 5 cells and stays uncolored anyway, so matching cell count alone doesn't fully resolve which shapes get colored.

So maybe it's about whether the marker clusters can actually be assembled into the target shape. In Ex2 the markers form a single cell plus two dominoes, which could combine into the cross shape's arms and center, so I'm checking whether the two tromino-shaped marker clusters in Ex1 could similarly tile shape A.

Testing shape A and B, both decompose cleanly into two L-trominoes matching the marker clusters. But Ex3's diagonal tromino marker can't tile a 3x3 block that way, so this tiling idea seems inconsistent—maybe it really just comes down to matching total cell counts.

Now checking ex2's L-shape rows more carefully, I count 5 cells forming an L, matching a marker count of 5, and confirming it's not connected to anything above it. This seems consistent with a size-matching rule, though I'm unsure why the cross shape gets selected specifically.

I try another angle: maybe symmetry matters, since a cross is symmetric but an L isn't. I check whether the ex1 shapes A and B are point-symmetric around their center, testing coordinate pairs against a rotation, but the check fails on one point. That symmetry idea doesn't quite hold either, so I decide to try a different classification approach based on shape color instead.
